newsitem.title: JAPAN: OLYMPICS-JAPANESE OFFICIAL BACKS DOWN ON SKATING CRITICISM.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-JAPANESE OFFICIAL BACKS DOWN ON SKATING CRITICISM.

text.p: A top Japanese Olympic official backed down on Wednesday after making disparaging remarks about speed skating in the Winter Games.

Goro Yoshimura, vice-president of the Nagano Olympic Committee and also governor of Nagano prefecture, site of the 1998 Winter Games, had said he believed spectators found Japanese-style open races more entertaining than Olympic-style timed races which he compared to "beetles on a whirligig".
"Since my remark drew controversy, I have announced that I withdraw it," said Yoshimura, himself a former speed skater.
"I used the Japanese word 'not interesting', but I didn't mean to criticise speed skaters or the sport itself."
But Yoshimura said he still believed races involving eight skaters were more exciting than Olympic-style races in which skaters race in pairs against the clock.
"But that's a personal opinion," he added.

Speed-skating races were conducted Japanese-style at the 1932 Lake Placid Winter Olympics in the United States, but fell out of favour after American skaters swept almost all the events, said Haruhiko Takano, senior adviser to the Nagano organising committee.
Other competitors accused the Americans of gaining unfair advantage by avoiding taking the lead, he said. Lead skaters shelter other competitors from headwinds.
The Japanese, who compete in hotly contested open races at their annual national sports festival, employ a different system to ensure fairness.
In order to win, skaters must lead the race a pre-determined number of times at the midway marks of the oval.
The requirement increases with distance. Skaters cannot win a 1,000-metre race unless they lead the race at least once. A 10,000-metre skater must lead at least eight times.
